procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 17th October, 2015 of the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Criminal Revision Application No.192 of 2014, setting aside the order of the trial court dated 22nd March, 2013 and discharging the respondent in Criminal Case No. 2.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent (Reliance Industries Ltd.) moved the High Court by way of a revision petition against the trial court's order dated 22nd March, 2013, which had rejected their application for discharge and framed charges. The High Court allowed the revision petition, setting aside the trial court's order and discharging the respondent. The High Court reasoned that since Rule 56A was omitted without a saving clause, the proceedings could not continue.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (Chandpaklal Ramanlal Shah and Anr.) appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the High Court, and restored the order of the trial court.

directions: The order of the High Court is set aside.
The order of the trial court is restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether the quashing of a charge for evasion of duty is justified merely on the ground that the procedural rule (Rule 56A), which was allegedly misused, was subsequently omitted without a saving clause.

facts: The respondent was facing a charge for evasion of duty.
The alleged evasion was committed by misusing Rule 56A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, to avail credit.
Subsequently, Rule 56A was omitted by a notification without a saving clause.
Based on this omission, the High Court quashed the charge against the respondent.
law: The primary and substantive offense is the evasion of duty itself.
A rule that outlines the method for availing credit (like Rule 56A) is considered a procedural rule.
application: The Supreme Court focused on the core nature of the charge, which was the act of evasion.
It reasoned that the omission of a procedural rule (Rule 56A) does not eliminate the underlying substantive offense of evasion.

The Court held that the prosecution must be given the opportunity to prove the evasion, as it is an offense in and of itself, irrespective of the later omission of the procedural rule that was allegedly misused to commit it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the charge. The omission of the procedural Rule 56A did not invalidate the charge for the substantive offense of duty evasion.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the quashing of a charge for evasion of duty is justified merely on the ground that the procedural rule (Rule 56A), which was allegedly misused, was subsequently omitted without a saving clause.
appellant_arguments: The charge against the respondent was for evasion of excise duty under Section 9(1)(b), a provision which remains unamended.
The evasion was a result of the respondent taking credit without following the procedure laid out in Rule 56A.
The subsequent omission of Rule 56A does not legally invalidate the charge for an offense committed when the rule was in force.
respondent_arguments: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, which saves proceedings under repealed statutes, does not apply to an 'omission' of a rule, only to a 'repeal' of an Act or Regulation.
In view of the Explanation to Section 132 of the Finance Act, 2001, the prosecution could not continue as there was no retrospective validation for it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The omission of a procedural rule does not invalidate a charge for a substantive offense, such as evasion of duty, when the core ingredient of the offense is the substantive act itself.
obiter: Whether Section 6 of the General Clauses Act applies to the omission of a rule.
The effect of retrospective amendments on prosecutions under an omitted rule.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central reasoning is that the substantive charge against the respondent is for the evasion of duty, and the core ingredient of this offense is the act of evasion itself. The subsequent omission of Rule 56A, which was merely the procedural rule allegedly misused to facilitate the evasion, does not affect the validity of the charge for the underlying substantive offense. The court determined that the disappearance of a procedural mechanism cannot retroactively nullify an offense committed when that mechanism was in force.
legal_tests_applied: Distinguishing between a substantive offense (evasion of duty) and the procedural rule (Rule 56A) used to facilitate the offense.
policy_considerations: The prosecution cannot be deprived of the opportunity to prove evasion, which is an offense in itself, merely because a procedural rule was later omitted.
